entries.name: X.509 and PKI
entries.summary: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by an issuer. A chain of such signatures up to a trusted root is what lets a client trust a server.

started.basis: RFC 5280 publication (the current X.509 profile for the Internet)

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF and ITU, not a CNCF project.

version.name: X.509 profile (RFC 5280)
version.docs: datatracker.ietf.org RFC 5280 (first 100,000 of 391,511 characters read) and CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3

compare.text: X.509 is the certificate format. TLS is the protocol that sends and checks it.

notes: RFC 5280 is dated May 2008, the day is not on the page. Only the first 100,000 of 391,511 characters were read, so path validation (section 6), Basic Constraints, Subject Alternative Name, Extended Key Usage, CRL Distribution Points and Authority Information Access details were not read.

The ballot page states the eventual 47-day and 10-day figures and March 2026 to March 2029 only. It does not state the intermediate steps (200 and 100 days), which are therefore not listed here (unconfirmed).

sections.title: In one minute
items: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by an issuer. A chain of such signatures up to a trusted root is what lets a client trust a server.

items.alt: A leaf certificate for a website is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA. The client's trust store holds the root. The server sends the leaf and the intermediate.
items.caption: A chain of trust. The client needs the root in its trust store and the intermediates from the server.

cards.title: Certificate
cards.text: Three fields: `tbsCertificate` (the part that is signed), `signatureAlgorithm` and `signatureValue`.

cards.title: Names
cards.text: The subject name can be in the subject field, the subjectAltName extension, or both. Put every host name in subjectAltName.

cards.title: Chain
cards.text: From the server certificate through intermediates to a trust anchor in the client's trust store.

cards.title: Validity
cards.text: Dates in the certificate. Lifetimes are getting shorter: see Run it.

sections.title: Read one

items.title: Print a certificate, its subjectAltName and its subject

items: More ways to read, test and fix certificates are in [Inspect and troubleshoot](#troubleshooting).

sections.title: What is inside (RFC 5280)
items: A `tbsCertificate` holds version, serialNumber, signature, issuer, validity, subject, subjectPublicKeyInfo and extensions. The signature covers the DER-encoded `tbsCertificate`.
The serial number is a positive integer, unique per issuer, at most 20 octets. Version 3 is required when extensions are present.
Validity dates use UTCTime until 2049 and GeneralizedTime from 2050. A certificate with no expiry uses `99991231235959Z`.
Each extension is marked critical or non-critical, and a system must reject a certificate with a critical extension it does not recognise.
CAs must support key identifiers, basic constraints, key usage and certificate policies. If `keyCertSign` is set in key usage, basic constraints must say `cA`.

If the subject carries only SAN identities such as an email or a URI, the subject is empty and `subjectAltName` must be critical. The `emailAddress` attribute in the subject is deprecated in favour of an `rfc822Name` in `subjectAltName`.

sections.title: Chains, trust and revocation
items: A client builds a chain from the server certificate through intermediates to a trust anchor in its trust store. OpenSSL does not ship a default set of trust anchors: you give it one. Intermediates you supply are used to build a path but are not trust anchors.

items.text: Chain building fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate" when the trust store has neither the root nor an unbroken chain to it. See Inspect and troubleshoot.

items: A CRL is a signed, time-stamped list of revoked certificates by serial number. The profile does not require CRLs: OCSP and other mechanisms are allowed.
Short lifetimes make revocation less necessary: OpenBao's PKI docs say short TTLs keep CRLs short.

rows: Maximum TLS certificate validity goes from 398 days to 47 days, and domain validation data reuse for SANs from 398 days to 10 days. Reductions are proposed to start in March 2026 and finish in March 2029
Default profile moves to 64-day certificates on 2027-02-10 and 45-day certificates on 2028-02-16, from 90 days today

items.text: Short lifetimes make automatic renewal necessary, so use [ACME](#acme) or an operator such as [cert-manager](#cert-manager).
items.title: What to do

items.text: The ballot page states only the eventual 47-day and 10-day figures and March 2026 to March 2029. The intermediate steps (200 and 100 days) are not on the page, so they are not listed.
items.unconfirmed: Not on the ballot page read.

entries.name: TLS
entries.summary: The protocol that uses certificates to encrypt and authenticate a connection. TLS 1.3 is current. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

version.name: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and RFC 8996
version.docs: datatracker.ietf.org RFC 8446 (first 100,000 of 386,953 characters read), RFC 8996, openssl s_client docs

notes: RFC 8446 date is August 2018 and RFC 8996 March 2021; the days are not on the pages read. version.released is the first of the month.
The RFC 8446 page was read only up to 100,000 of 386,953 characters. ALPN and certificate selection details are not covered (unconfirmed).

sections.title: In one minute
items: TLS is the protocol that uses certificates to encrypt and authenticate a connection. TLS 1.3 is current. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated.

items.alt: The TLS 1.3 handshake takes one round trip: ClientHello from the client, then ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished from the server, then Finished from the client. Application data follows.
items.caption: TLS 1.3 handshake, one round trip. Everything after ServerHello is encrypted.

rows: "TLS 1.0 MUST NOT be used". DTLS 1.0 is deprecated too, DTLS 1.2 is not

sections.title: What happens in the handshake
items: Messages: ClientHello and ServerHello, then EncryptedExtensions, an optional CertificateRequest, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished. Everything after ServerHello is encrypted.
The full handshake takes one round trip. Key exchange is (EC)DHE, PSK-only, or PSK with (EC)DHE.

items.text: 0-RTT: a client with a shared PSK can send early data in its first flight. That data is not forward secret and the RFC states there is no guarantee against replay between connections.
items.title: 0-RTT early data

items: Removed in TLS 1.3: static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman suites, compression, DSA, custom DHE groups, renegotiation and non-AEAD ciphers.

sections.title: Certificates in the handshake
items: The server always authenticates with a certificate. Client authentication is optional: the server asks with `CertificateRequest` and the client replies with its own Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished. That is mutual TLS (mTLS).
The client sends the name it wants in the SNI extension, so one address can serve several certificates. `openssl s_client` sets SNI from `-connect` when it is a DNS name, or from `-servername`.
The certificate must name the host in its `subjectAltName`. See [X.509 and PKI](#x509).

entries.name: Certificate and key formats
entries.summary: PEM (text), DER (binary), PKCS#12 (a container with certificate and key) and CSRs. Most 'it does not load' problems are the wrong format.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF and RSA, not a CNCF project.

version.name: RFC 7468, openssl pkcs12 and openssl req docs

notes: RFC 7468 is dated April 2015; the day is not on the page. JKS, the Java key store, is not covered (unconfirmed).

sections.title: PEM (RFC 7468)
items: Text: a line -----BEGIN <label>----- then the base64 of a DER structure, then -----END <label>-----. The base64 is wrapped at 64 characters by generators.
Labels: CERTIFICATE, X509 CRL, CERTIFICATE REQUEST (a PKCS#10 CSR), PKCS7, CMS, PRIVATE KEY (an unencrypted PKCS#8 key), ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY, ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE, PUBLIC KEY.
A file can hold several blocks, for example a certificate followed by its intermediates. DER is the binary form.

sections.title: PKCS#12 (PFX)
items: A container for certificates and private keys, used by Windows and some browsers and mail clients. Azure Key Vault returns a certificate with its key as PFX or PEM.
Create: openssl pkcs12 -export -in cert.pem -inkey key.pem -out file.p12, with -certfile for extra CA certificates and -name for a friendly name.
Convert to PEM: openssl pkcs12 -in file.p12 -out file.pem. Private keys come out encrypted unless you add -noenc. The older -nodes is deprecated since OpenSSL 3.0.
OpenSSL 3 defaults to AES-256-CBC with PBKDF2, SHA256 for the MAC and 2048 iterations. Old files using RC2 or 3DES need -legacy.

sections.title: Making a CSR or a self-signed certificate
items: openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -noenc -keyout key.pem -out req.csr -subj "/C=GB/CN=foo.example.com" -addext "subjectAltName = DNS:foo.example.com"
Add -x509 and -days to get a self-signed certificate instead (default 30 days). Put every host name in subjectAltName.

entries.name: ACME and Let's Encrypt
entries.summary: The protocol (RFC 8555) that lets software prove it controls a domain and get a certificate automatically. Let's Encrypt is the best known free ACME CA.

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

entries.maintainer: IETF ACME working group; Let's Encrypt is run by ISRG

version.name: ACME (RFC 8555) and Let's Encrypt docs
version.docs: datatracker.ietf.org RFC 8555 (first 100,000 of 221,975 characters read), letsencrypt.org docs

compare.text: cert-manager runs the ACME protocol for Kubernetes workloads. ACME alone is what the other clients speak.

notes: Let's Encrypt's launch date is not on the pages read, so it is not stated (unconfirmed). Key authorization, certificate download and revocation sections of RFC 8555 were past the part read.
The Let's Encrypt lifetime dates are from its announcement page, which the page itself gives as future dates. The CA/Browser Forum schedule is separate; see X.509 and PKI.
RFC 8555 is dated March 2019; the day is not on the page. version.released is the first of the month.

sections.title: In one minute
items: ACME (RFC 8555) lets software prove it controls a domain and get a certificate automatically. Let's Encrypt, run by the nonprofit Internet Security Research Group, is the best known free ACME CA: anyone who owns a domain name can get a trusted certificate at zero cost.

items.alt: The ACME client creates an account and an order, receives a challenge, proves control of the domain by an HTTP file or a DNS record, finalizes the order and downloads the certificate.
items.caption: An ACME order.

cards.title: Account
cards.text: Holds contact details and the account public key. Statuses: valid, deactivated, revoked.

cards.title: Order
cards.text: A request for a certificate: pending, ready, processing, valid, invalid.

cards.title: Authorization and challenge
cards.text: Permission to act for an identifier, and a proof of control. The RFC defines `http-01` and `dns-01`.

cards.title: Directory
cards.text: One URL is all a client needs. It maps `newNonce`, `newAccount`, `newOrder`, `newAuthz`, `revokeCert` and `keyChange` to URLs.

rows: Port 80 reachable. With several servers the file must be on all of them. The simplest to automate
A DNS provider with an API. Storing its credentials on a web server is risky. Cannot validate IP addresses. Works for servers not exposed to the internet
Client support is limited. Described as not suitable for most people

sections.title: Try it against staging
items: Production: `https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory`. Use staging while testing because its limits are significantly higher.

sections.title: Clients
items: certbot, acme.sh and lego are standalone ACME clients. Caddy has ACME built in. cert-manager is the Kubernetes one. step-ca is an ACME server for a private CA, and Boulder is an ACME-based CA written in Go.
ZeroSSL is Caddy's fallback CA when Let's Encrypt fails.
See [cert-manager](#cert-manager) for Kubernetes.

sections.title: Protocol details (RFC 8555)
items: Requests are signed as a flattened JWS with the account key and sent as `application/jose+json`. Fetching data uses POST-as-GET. Every server response carries a single-use `Replay-Nonce`, and a rejected nonce returns `badNonce` with a fresh one.
The RFC defines the `http-01` and `dns-01` challenges. Revocation is a signed request to `revokeCert`.

rows: The default `classic` profile moves to 64 days
items.caption: Dates apply to new certificates.

rows: Authorization failures per identifier per hour

entries.name: Caddy
entries.summary: A web server that turns on HTTPS by itself: it gets and renews certificates from ACME CAs with no extra configuration.

sections.title: Automatic HTTPS
items: Turns on when Caddy knows a domain name or IP address to serve. It obtains and renews certificates and redirects HTTP to HTTPS on port 80.

Public names use ACME CAs: Let's Encrypt first and ZeroSSL as the fallback. Challenges: HTTP (port 80), TLS-ALPN (port 443) and DNS (TXT records, no open ports needed). When several are enabled Caddy picks one at random and favours those that succeed. Enabling DNS turns off the other two by default.
Localhost, IP addresses and similar names get certificates from Caddy's own local CA. Other clients do not trust them unless they have that root.
On-demand TLS gets a certificate during the first handshake for a new name. Restrict it, typically with an ask endpoint.
On failure Caddy retries, switches challenge types, then issuers, backing off up to one day between attempts for up to 30 days.

entries.name: step-ca
entries.summary: An open source online certificate authority for X.509 and SSH certificates, with an ACME server, from Smallstep.
notes: The page links to an installation section that was not read, so install methods are not listed. Smallstep is a company with a hosted product; only the open source CA is covered. Latest release v0.30.2 is from 2026-03-23.

sections.title: What it is
items: "An open source, online certificate authority for issuing and managing X.509 and SSH certificates"; the server counterpart of the step CLI.

Provisioners (how clients get certificates): ACME challenge responses from any ACMEv2 client, OAuth/OIDC ID tokens (Okta, Google Workspace, Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Dex), cloud instance identity documents (AWS, GCP, Azure), and single-use short-lived JWK tokens.
X.509 for TLS, mTLS and document signing with RSA, ECDSA or EdDSA keys, configurable lifetimes and templates. Short-lived certificates with automated renewal and passive revocation.

Built for a two-tier PKI with an offline root and an online intermediate, or an online intermediate under an existing root. Key protection through PKCS #11 HSMs, Google Cloud KMS, AWS KMS and YubiKey PIV.

sections.title: Documented limits
items: A single issuing intermediate, authority-wide issuance policies, limited active revocation (CRL, OCSP), and no Certificate Transparency integration, issuance history, dynamic SCEP or ACME External Account Binding.

entries.name: OpenBao
entries.summary: A secrets manager whose PKI secrets engine issues short-lived X.509 certificates on demand. A Linux Foundation project.
notes: The docs page footer reads "OpenBao a Series of LF Projects, LLC" and says it is a Sandbox project under OpenSSF. It does not say OpenBao is a fork of HashiCorp Vault, nor state a licence. MPL-2.0 is the SPDX id GitHub reports. The fork origin is widely reported but not on a page read (unconfirmed). HashiCorp Vault itself is not covered.
The page does not describe roles or ACME setup. Not a CNCF project.

sections.title: PKI secrets engine
items: Generates dynamic X.509 certificates, so a service gets one without generating a key and CSR, submitting it to a CA and waiting. Verification uses OpenBao's built in authentication and authorization.

Short TTLs make revocation less necessary, which keeps CRLs short and helps the engine scale. Each running instance can have its own certificate. Ephemeral certificates can be fetched into memory at startup and discarded at shutdown.
It has a full HTTP API. The docs link to guides for root CA, intermediate CA, CEL-based issue and sign policies, ACME troubleshooting and rotation.

entries.name: SPIFFE and SPIRE
entries.summary: SPIFFE is a set of standards for workload identity, with short-lived X.509 or JWT identity documents. SPIRE is its main implementation. CNCF graduated.

cncf.text: SPIRE was accepted to CNCF on March 29, 2018, moved to Incubating on June 22, 2020 and to Graduated on August 22, 2022.

notes: The overview page does not describe the SPIFFE ID format, so it is not given here. Start date is the first GitHub release.

sections.title: What it is
items: SPIFFE: open standards that give software systems verifiable identities so they can authenticate each other wherever they run. The core specification defines short-lived cryptographic identity documents, SVIDs.
Two SVID types: X.509-SVIDs (certificates) and JWT-SVIDs (tokens). A Workload API delivers them to workloads.
SPIRE is the main open source implementation, covering X.509-SVIDs, JWT-SVIDs, attestation-based issuance, the Workload API and federation on Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal.

entries.name: mkcert
entries.summary: Makes locally trusted development certificates with any names, with no configuration. For development only.
notes: Status is a judgement: the latest release is v1.4.4 from 2022-04-26 and the last push to the repository was 2024-08-13. It is still widely used for local development (unconfirmed). Never use the local CA outside your own machine.

sections.title: What it is
items: "A simple tool for making locally-trusted development certificates. It requires no configuration." mkcert -install creates a local CA and installs it in the system and Firefox trust stores. mkcert example.com "*.example.com" localhost 127.0.0.1 ::1 writes a certificate and key valid for those names.

entries.name: cert-manager
entries.summary: A Kubernetes operator that creates TLS certificates for workloads and renews them before they expire, from ACME CAs, private CAs, Vault and others. CNCF graduated.

cncf.text: cert-manager was accepted to CNCF on November 10, 2020, moved to Incubating on September 19, 2022 and to Graduated on September 29, 2024.

compare.text: certbot gets a certificate for one host. cert-manager manages many certificates as Kubernetes objects and renews them.
cert-manager is a client in the cluster. step-ca is a CA server that cert-manager can use as an ACME issuer.

notes: Start date is the first GitHub release. The default renewBefore is not stated as a number on the page; the 2/3 figure is the page's description.
Gateway API support was not described on the ingress page read (unconfirmed). The cmctl and kubectl cert-manager status commands were not on the troubleshooting page.
Install pages were read for v1.21.3, the same as the latest release.

sections.title: In one minute
items: cert-manager is a Kubernetes operator that "creates TLS certificates for workloads in your Kubernetes or OpenShift cluster" and renews them before they expire. It is a CNCF graduated project.

items.alt: An Ingress with an issuer annotation makes cert-manager create a Certificate. The Certificate creates a CertificateRequest, which for ACME creates an Order and a Challenge. The result is stored in a Secret that the Ingress uses.
items.caption: The resource chain for an ACME certificate.

cards.title: Issuer, ClusterIssuer
cards.text: Where certificates come from. An Issuer works in one namespace, a ClusterIssuer cluster-wide. Types: ACME (Let's Encrypt), CA (private PKI), HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk Certificate Manager (the URLs say venafi), SelfSigned, and external issuers.

cards.title: Certificate
cards.text: What you want: names, duration, issuer. cert-manager keeps the key and certificate in a Secret.

cards.title: Renewal
cards.text: Renews before expiry, at 2/3 of the lifetime by default.

cards.title: Related projects
cards.text: trust-manager, approver-policy, the webhook and CA Injector. csi-driver, csi-driver-spiffe or istio-csr generate the key on demand and never store it in a Secret.

sections.title: Install it

items.title: Install with Helm from the OCI registry

items: The OCI registry is recommended and is the source of truth, published immediately on release. The legacy repository (`helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io`) is updated a few hours later. You can also use `kubectl apply`, or continuous deployment (GitOps).

items.text: Install it once. Do not embed cert-manager as a subchart, because it manages cluster-scoped resources.

sections.title: Create an issuer
items: `spec.acme` has `email`, `server` (the ACME directory URL), `privateKeySecretRef` (the account key Secret) and `solvers`.

Solvers use `http01` (for example `ingress.ingressClassName: nginx`) or `dns01` with a provider such as `cloudflare` or `cloudDNS`. The docs list ACMEDNS, Akamai, AzureDNS, DigitalOcean, RFC-2136, Route53 and Webhook as well.

items.text: Test with the staging server `https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory` first.

sections.title: Get a certificate for an Ingress
items: Annotate the Ingress with `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer` (a ClusterIssuer, any namespace) or `cert-manager.io/issuer` (an Issuer in the same namespace), and add `spec.tls` with `hosts` and a unique `secretName`.
The ingress-shim component watches Ingresses with a supported annotation and creates a Certificate named after `secretName`. `hosts` become the subjectAltNames.
The page notes ingress-nginx is scheduled for end of life in March 2026.

rows: required: the Secret for the certificate and key, in the same namespace
the SANs. At least one of commonName, dnsNames, uris, emailAddresses, ipAddresses or otherNames is required
defaults to 90 days (2160h). Minimum 1 hour, and greater than `renewBefore`
renewal happens at 2/3 of the lifetime by default. Minimum effective value 5 minutes

sections.title: What ends up in the Secret
items: `tls.crt` (certificate and chain), `tls.key` and `ca.crt` (not present with ACME).
A change to names, usages, duration or issuerRef triggers reissuance. `cmctl renew` forces it.

items.text: Deleting the Secret is not recommended.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
items: In order: `kubectl get` and `describe` certificate, then certificaterequest, then the issuer or clusterissuer, then for ACME the order and challenge. Read Status and Events first, logs only if those do not help.
Example: a Certificate with Reason `DoesNotExist` and "Issuing certificate as Secret does not exist" is still waiting for issuance.

entries.summary: Where certificates appear in a cluster: TLS for Ingress, the CertificateSigningRequest API, and the cluster's own certificates managed by kubeadm.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Where certificates appear in a cluster: TLS for Ingress, the CertificateSigningRequest API, and the cluster's own certificates managed by kubeadm.

items.alt: A client creates a CertificateSigningRequest naming a signer. An approver approves it. The signing controller writes the certificate into status.certificate, and the client fetches it.
items.caption: The CertificateSigningRequest lifecycle.

sections.title: Ingress TLS
items: An Ingress "may provide load balancing, SSL termination and name-based virtual hosting" through its controller. The Kubernetes project recommends Gateway instead of Ingress and the Ingress API is frozen: generally available, with no further development.

With [cert-manager](#cert-manager), `spec.tls` lists `hosts` and a `secretName`. cert-manager stores the issued certificate in that Secret and the hosts become the SANs. Each Ingress needs a unique `secretName`.

sections.title: The CertificateSigningRequest API
items: `certificates.k8s.io/v1`. `spec.request` holds a base64-encoded PEM PKCS#10 request. `spec.signerName` is required in v1.
`spec.expirationSeconds` (v1.22 and later) requests a lifetime, minimum 600 seconds. Approval and signing need separate RBAC permissions (`approve` and `sign` on the `signers` resource).
Cleanup: approved, denied or failed requests are removed after 1 hour, pending ones after 24 hours, and any after the issued certificate expires.

sections.title: kubeadm cluster certificates
items: External CA mode: give kubeadm only `ca.crt`, not `ca.key`. Run the controller manager with `--controllers=csrsigner` pointing at the CA.
Custom certificates: put your own pairs in `certificatesDir` (default `/etc/kubernetes/pki`) before `kubeadm init`. kubeadm does not overwrite existing pairs.

items.text: kubeadm upgrade renews control plane certificates by default (from general knowledge).
items.unconfirmed: Not in the part of the page read.

sections.title: Where cert-manager and SPIFFE fit
items: Use [cert-manager](#cert-manager) for workload and ingress certificates and for renewal. SPIRE issues short-lived workload identity certificates (X.509-SVIDs).

entries.name: Azure Key Vault certificates
entries.summary: Azure's managed store for X.509 certificates: create or import them, manage their lifecycle with a policy, and renew automatically with partner CAs.

started.basis: Not stated on the page read

cncf.text: Commercial service, not a CNCF project.

notes: Included as a cloud reference. It is not open source. The page does not state a start date or a price.

sections.title: What it does
items: Create a certificate in the vault or import one (self-signed or CA issued). Secure storage of X.509 certificates without handling the private key. A policy directs Key Vault to manage the lifecycle, and contacts get notifications about expiry and renewal.
Automatic renewal works with partner issuers: DigiCert and GlobalSign. Other providers and CAs are allowed but do not auto-renew.

Creating a certificate also creates a key and a secret with the same name. The secret returns the certificate with its private key as PFX or PEM, only if the policy says the key is exportable. Exportable keys are RSA and EC only, and HSM keys are non-exportable.
Policy: subject and SANs, key type and length, exportable, ReuseKeyOnRenewal, and lifetime actions that trigger by days before expiry or percentage of lifetime and do emailContacts or autoRenew.
Publicly trusted certificates are submitted to Certificate Transparency logs outside Azure during enrolment. Key Vault has no CT toggle.

sections.title: What it does
items: Handles creating, storing and renewing public and private SSL/TLS X.509 certificates for AWS websites and applications. Issue directly from ACM or import third-party certificates.
Certificates can cover one name, several names or wildcards. Wildcards protect any number of subdomains.
You are not charged extra for the certificates you manage with ACM; you pay for the AWS resources that use them.

Certificates are regional. For Elastic Load Balancing in several regions you request or import one per region and revalidate the names. For CloudFront the certificate must be in US East (N. Virginia).
For publicly trusted certificates on standalone servers such as EC2, the page points to ACME certificate automation. ACM certificates signed by AWS Private CA can be exported.

sections.title: Read a certificate

items.title: Print, expiry-check and fingerprint a certificate

items: `-noout` with `-subject`, `-issuer`, `-dates` (start and end) or `-enddate` prints just those fields. Add `-inform DER` for a binary file.
`-checkend 86400` exits nonzero if the certificate expires within that many seconds, which suits a monitoring check.

sections.title: Test a server
items: `-servername` sets SNI. Without it, SNI comes from `-connect` when that is a DNS name. `-showcerts` prints the certificates the server sent, in the order sent. That is not a verified chain: it shows whether the server sends its intermediates.

`-CAfile`, `-CApath` or `-CAstore` load trust anchors. `-verify_return_error` aborts the handshake on a verification error, otherwise errors are shown and the command carries on. `-brief` prints a short summary.
`-tls1_2` and `-tls1_3` pick a version. `-starttls protocol` (smtp, imap, pop3, ftp, postgres, mysql, ldap and others) upgrades a plain connection first.

sections.title: Verify a chain
items: `-CAfile root.pem` loads trusted roots. OpenSSL does not provide a default set of trust anchors. `-untrusted intermediates.pem` supplies intermediates, which help build a path but are never trust anchors.

`-purpose sslserver` checks the certificate's extensions against its intended use. `-verify_hostname name` checks a DNS name in the SAN, or the common name. `-attime` sets another reference time and `-no_check_time` skips the validity check.

sections.title: Make a CSR or a self-signed certificate

items.title: Pack a key and certificate into PKCS#12

rows: unable to get local issuer certificate
Chain building failed. The trust store has neither the root nor an unbroken chain to it. The usual cause is a server that does not send its intermediate: install the full chain
Trusted only if it is in the trust store and is a trust anchor. Add it to the store, or use a real CA
Validity is checked at each element of the chain against the current time. Check the clock and the dates with `-dates`
The name is not in the certificate's identity fields. Put every host name in `subjectAltName`
items.caption: Numeric X509 error codes are not on the OpenSSL pages read, so they are not listed here.

sections.title: cert-manager
items: In order: `kubectl get` and `describe` certificate, then certificaterequest, then the issuer or clusterissuer, then for ACME the order and challenge. Look at Status and Events first and logs last. `kubectl get event` shows the namespace's events.
Chain: Ingress (optional), Certificate, CertificateRequest, Order, Challenge.
